question: How far forward should a rider sit in the seat to control the motorcycle well?
choice_a: Far enough forward that the arms are slightly bent when holding the handgrips
choice_c: Standing on the footrests at all times
choice_d: Seat position doesn't matter for control
explanation: Sit far enough forward so that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips; bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without having to reach too far.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.13, 'Body Position'

question: How should a rider position their wrist at the start, and why?
choice_a: Bend the right wrist sharply upward for maximum throttle control
choice_b: Start with the right wrist flat, to help avoid accidentally using too much throttle
choice_c: Wrist position has no effect on throttle control
choice_d: Keep both wrists loose and dangling
explanation: Start with your right wrist flat -- this helps keep you from accidentally using too much throttle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.13, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the manual recommend keeping your knees against the gas tank?
choice_c: To help keep your balance as the motorcycle turns
explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank to help keep your balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.13, 'Body Position'

question: Why should a rider keep their feet firmly on the footrests rather than letting the toes point downward?
choice_a: To make the ride more comfortable only
choice_c: So the rider can reach the ground while moving
choice_d: To maintain balance and avoid the toes getting caught between the road and the footrests
explanation: Keep your feet firmly on the footrests to maintain balance; don't let your toes point downward -- they may get caught between the road and the footrests.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.13, 'Body Position'

question: In a typical 1-N-2-3-4-5 gear pattern, how is neutral (N) selected?
choice_a: By a half-lift from 1st gear or a half-press from 2nd gear
choice_b: By pressing the shift lever all the way down from 1st gear
choice_c: Neutral is never located between 1st and 2nd gear
choice_d: By pulling in the clutch and releasing it fully
explanation: In a typical 1-N-2-3-4-5 gear pattern, N (neutral) is selected by either a half lift from 1st gear or a half press from 2nd gear.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.13, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What is the correct 3-step process for upshifting?
choice_a: Roll on the throttle, then shift, then squeeze the clutch
choice_b: Roll off the throttle while squeezing the clutch, lift the shift lever firmly and release, then smoothly ease out the clutch lever and adjust the throttle
choice_c: Shift first, then squeeze the clutch
choice_d: There is no set process for upshifting
explanation: When upshifting, use a 3-step process: 1) roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever, 2) lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go and release, 3) smoothly ease out the clutch lever and adjust the throttle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What happens if you shift into a lower gear while riding too fast for that gear?
choice_a: Nothing -- speed has no effect on downshifting
choice_b: The engine will always stall immediately
choice_c: The motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid
choice_d: The front wheel will lock automatically
explanation: You must be riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear; if not, the motorcycle will lurch, and the rear wheel may skid.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What effect does shifting to a lower gear and easing out the clutch (engine braking) have on a motorcycle?
choice_a: It has no effect on speed
choice_b: It only works when the motorcycle is stopped
choice_c: It instantly locks the rear wheel
choice_d: It causes an effect similar to using the brakes, slowing the motorcycle
explanation: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes, known as engine braking; to use it, shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between each downshift.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Shifting Gears'

question: Why should a rider remain in first gear while stopped?
choice_a: So they can move out quickly if needed
choice_c: First gear is required by law while stopped
choice_d: It has no benefit; any gear works the same
explanation: Remain in first gear while you are stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Shifting Gears'

question: How much of a motorcycle's total stopping power can the front brake provide when applied properly?
choice_d: None -- the front brake should never be used
explanation: Most motorcycles have two brake controls; the front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power, and is safe to use if used properly.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Braking'

question: How is maximum straight-line braking accomplished?
choice_a: By using the rear brake only
choice_b: By using the front brake only
choice_c: By fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
choice_d: By coasting to a stop without using either brake
explanation: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.14, 'Braking'

question: What should a rider do to prevent a rear-wheel skid while braking normally?
choice_a: Slam down hard on the rear brake pedal
choice_b: Only use the rear brake and avoid the front brake entirely
choice_c: Release the rear brake completely at all times
choice_d: Apply light-to-lighter pressure to the rear brake pedal as weight transfers forward
explanation: Apply light-to-lighter pressure to the rear brake pedal to prevent a rear-wheel skid; as weight transfers forward, less traction is available at the rear.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.15, 'Braking'

question: Any time a motorcycle is leaned over, what happens to the traction available for braking?
choice_a: It is reduced -- the greater the lean angle, the more likely the tires are to lose traction
choice_b: It increases as the lean angle increases
choice_c: Lean angle has no effect on available traction
choice_d: Traction is only affected by tire pressure, not lean angle
explanation: Any time a motorcycle is leaned over, the amount of traction available for braking is reduced -- the greater the lean angle, the more the possibility of the tires losing traction.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.15, 'Braking in a Corner'

question: What is Anti-Lock Braking System (ABS) designed to do?
choice_b: Prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations
choice_c: Replace the need for a front brake
explanation: ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations; if electronic sensors detect a possible wheel lock, brake pressure is released and then reapplied.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.15, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: According to the manual, how many times per second is ABS capable of releasing and reapplying brake pressure?
explanation: ABS is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.15, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: What is the correct 4-step process (SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL) for turning effectively?
choice_a: Look down at the front wheel, brake hard, then release the handlebars
choice_b: Accelerate into the turn before looking
choice_c: Turn the handlebars sharply without leaning
choice_d: Slow before the turn, look through the turn, press the handgrip in the direction of the turn to lean, then roll on the throttle to stabilize
explanation: The four steps are: SLOW (reduce speed before the turn), LOOK (look through the turn to where you want to go), PRESS (press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn to lean the motorcycle), and ROLL (roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed and stabilize the motorcycle).
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.15-16, 'Turning'

question: To turn left, which handgrip should a rider press, and what happens?
choice_a: Press the left handgrip -- lean left -- go left
choice_b: Press the right handgrip to go left
choice_c: Pull back on both handgrips equally
choice_d: Handgrip pressure has no effect on direction
explanation: To turn, the motorcycle must lean: press the left handgrip to lean left and go left; press the right handgrip to lean right and go right. This is known as countersteering.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.16, 'Turning'

question: In slow, tight turns, how should a rider and the motorcycle be positioned, compared to normal turns?
choice_a: Lean the rider's body only while keeping the motorcycle upright
choice_b: Counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only while keeping the body upright
choice_c: Lean the rider and motorcycle together at the same steep angle, just like a normal turn
choice_d: Neither the rider nor the motorcycle should lean at all
explanation: In regular turns, the rider and motorcycle should lean together at the same angle. In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.16, 'Turning'
